newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German court awards RWE some damages.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German court awards RWE some damages.

text.p: A German court on Thursday ruled that a western German state must pay some damages to utility firm RWE AG after years of delays to the operation of a nuclear power plant.

While giving some credence to RWE's claims, the court did not award the utility the full seven billion marks ($4.39 billion) it was seeking and both the company and Rheinland Palatinate state officials said they were content with the ruling.

RWE had demanded damages for its initial investment, lost profits and cost of maintaining the huge station along the Rhine river at Muelheim Kaerlich, near Koblenz in western Germany, which has lain idle for almost a decade.

Rheinland Palatinate premier Kurt Beck, whose Social Democrats (SPD) form the main opposition in Bonn, said the decision was a victory for the state because the court ruled that RWE could not back up its full claim for damages.
"The damages (to RWE) are not quantifiable and also not that big," Beck told reporters.

The Federal Supreme Court in Karlsruhe said the state was liable for costs accrued by RWE in building and financing the plant and those associated with lost business, but not for the full duration of its inactivity.
The court also said RWE did not have to be compensated for lost profits. The state high court in Koblenz will later determine the exact level of damages.
RWE also said it was not unhappy with the ruling. "We are not dissatisfied with the judgement," said Harald Schueren, spokesman for RWE Energie AG, its energy subsidiary.
The company's shares rose to touch a high of 70 marks after the decision, up 1.60 marks, or 2.3 percent, but then slipped back to close bourse trade at 68.80 marks, up 40 pfennigs.
One dealer said that the hopes for damages in the billions of marks for RWE would probably not be fulfilled.

State environment minister Klaudia Martini said the decision meant that RWE had not got what it wanted. She said she thought that damages would not automatically be awarded to RWE when the case was passed on to the state court.
As a result of the case, Martini said she doubted whether state goverments would approve such large projects in future without protecting themselves against possible damage claims.
The environmentalist Greens party hailed the ruling as a great success for the anti-nuclear movement and demanded the the plant be torn down.
"In the future it will hopefully be more difficult to push through dinosaur projects of such a huge scale," the party said in a statement.
Building the plant was authorised in 1975, when Chancellor Helmut Kohl was premier of the state.
The Greens accused Kohl of burdening tax payers with the costs of a confused nuclear energy policy.

In 1988, after less than a year of trial operations, the 1,300 megawatt plant was forced to shut down because over a legal technicality and public concerns about whether it could survive an earthquake.
It has stood idle ever since and RWE put the cost of maintining the plant at 200 million marks each year.
"It's a German speciality to hold up authorisation in such a legal jungle," said Manfred Petroll, spokesman for the German Atom Forum, the nuclear energy industry's main lobby group.

The legal battle over the plant is still not over. Last week the Federal administrative court in Berlin said a revision of the original authorisation should be allowed, meaning that the plant could finally come on stream.
Muelheim-Kaerlich is the second RWE reactor to fall foul of legal and political wrangling.

Another nuclear plant, at Kalkar, near the Dutch border, was closed down in 1991 and is now the site of a planned amusement park. That plant, which cost seven billion marks but never generated a watt of electricity for consumers, was the focus of anti-nuclear protests in the 1980s.
